rv.q: Cardiac organs are pounding like crazy at After Midnight, the raucous, joyous, white-hot revue in which a ridiculously talented array of dancers, singers and ace musicians (handpicked by Wynton Marsalis) are whipping up a hurricane of fun.
The show succeeds triumphantly on all three counts.
Ninety minutes of exuberantly entertaining song and dance, this is a show that renders it impossible to keep your toes from tapping.
It will be a long time before Broadway hosts music making this hot, sweet and altogether glorious again.
At last comes “After Midnight,” a sleek, elegant tribute to Duke Ellington and the glory days of the Cotton Club that brings class back to Broadway.
Sanitized though it may be, “After Midnight” is great entertainment.
Those issues are so brushed aside, they feel here like the elephant in the cupboard.
Broadway patrons seeking a luscious sampler needn't travel further north than 47th Street, where the Theatre is jumpin', stompin' and downright roof raisin'
Instead, you get 90 minutes of honest, vital entertainment, delivered with enough breezy wit to mitigate the flashes of pomp.
The cast of “After Midnight” makes you feel as if you’re cozied up to a small table with your main squeeze and a gin fizz, feet away from Ellington and the band.
It's an exhilarating joyride all the way.
After Midnight is a celebration of Harlem's Cotton Club era that brings together exceptional dancing, singing, and musicianship in a thrilling night of entertainment.
The sensational Karine Plantadit, dancing to the Ellington masterpiece “Black and Tan Fantasy,” is the high point of the show.
After Midnight is a show that's as light on its feet as its very talented ensemble.
As staged by Warren Carlyle, "After Midnight" brings lively and snazzy period entertainment to Broadway with phenomenal sound, effervescent movement and a joyous spirit.

Called 'Cotton Club Parade,' it was initially a collaboration between the Jazz at Lincoln Center program and the New York City Center, and was performed at the City Center for brief runs in 2011 and 2012. The emergent 'After Midnight' is not your typical Broadway musical. But, taken on its own terms, it's thoroughly entertaining.
It‘s a delight, a pastiche of old jazz standards, dancing, glitter and feathers (costumes by Isabel Toledo).

cn.t: Critics hail this Duke Ellington-era revue as dazzling and exhilarating, praising its superb jazz orchestra, spirited choreography, and talented performers. Some note it feels sanitized or "Broadway-ized," but most find it elegantly entertaining.

sg.ra: Lena Horne is one of the smaller Nederlander houses (1,069 seats) and the front orchestra AAA/AA rows sit unusually close to the stage with an unraked front section — TripAdvisor reviewer in Row C reported head-blockage from the flat rake, so row B center is the sweet spot for SIX-style concert staging.

Mezzanine overhang at Lena Horne starts at Row J (Headout/TickPick), so rows E-I stay fully open to the ceiling — critical here because the house has only 18 orchestra rows (AAA-Q) and the overhang drops in early relative to larger Nederlander houses.

Headout and TickPick both pin mezzanine overhang start at Row J — with only 18 orchestra rows total, roughly the back half of the Lena Horne orchestra sits under that overhang and loses upper-stage visibility; NYTix specifically flags the side orchestra seats as 'aren't very comfortable'.

Lena Horne's front mezz is unusually shallow — only 4 rows (A-D) per BroadwayDirect chart — so even Row D sits close to the stage with 'advantageous' sightlines (Headout), and the bar is on the mezzanine level (NYTix) making this the most practical tier in this Nederlander house.

Because the front mezz only has 4 rows at Lena Horne, 'rear' of front mezz (C-D) is still just 3-4 rows from the rail — AVFMS R-D-16 and R-C-26 both reported clear views, and these are priced as value seats while Row A commands premium.

Rear mezz at Lena Horne is 8 rows (E-M) continuous with the front mezz balcony — there's no secondary overhang above it (Broadway-show-tickets.com), and because the house only holds 1,069 seats, AVFMS reviewer in Rear Mezz L row G called it 'excellent vantage without feeling far removed'.

Lena Horne's boxes sit tight to the proscenium of this narrow 1,069-seat Nederlander house, and both NYTix and TickPick explicitly warn the angle is 'extremely skewed' / 'more side-on' — private but not viable for shows with choreography or full-stage staging like SIX.
